episode_title: S2 E14 - How to Track Driver Hours When You Pay by the Mile

real_qa.q: What are California's requirements for tracking driver hours when paying by the mile?
real_qa.r: California requires separate compensation for nonproductive time such as pre-trip inspections, waiting to load, and qualified rest periods. These hours cannot be counted in mileage-only pay; they must be tracked separately and paid according to applicable wage requirements. Simply paying a high mileage rate does not automatically satisfy these requirements—all work hours must be accounted for and paid correctly.
real_qa.requete: California pay by the mile driver hours requirements

real_qa.q: How should trucking companies structure ELD activity categories to capture all required work time?
real_qa.r: A practical starting point includes: driving, inspections and fueling combined with other work, waiting with sufficient description, and meal or off-duty time. The key is using a small set of categories that drivers understand and payroll can use. Waiting entries need enough detail to explain circumstances—for example, whether the driver was released to leave or required to remain with the truck.
real_qa.requete: ELD activity categories trucking payroll time tracking

real_qa.q: What is the difference between a customer's detention billing policy and a driver's work time for pay purposes?
real_qa.r: A customer agreement stating detention billing begins after two hours is a billing arrangement only and does not determine whether the driver's first two hours count as paid work. Under California wage rules, drivers must be paid for all work time regardless of the customer's detention policy. Even if a shipper charges detention only after two hours, the driver must be paid for all time spent performing duties.
real_qa.requete: detention billing vs driver work time pay California

real_qa.q: How can tracking complete driver work hours improve business decisions beyond payroll compliance?
real_qa.r: Time tracking reveals that two identical 500-mile loads may have very different costs—one with a quick turnaround versus another with four hours of waiting. This data enables better conversations about pricing and scheduling, helps prioritize which customers to accept, and clarifies why drivers complain about certain routes. It shows that effective hourly earnings matter more than rate per mile alone.
real_qa.requete: trucking driver hours data pricing customer selection

real_qa.q: Why is dividing mileage earnings by total work hours insufficient to prove California wage compliance?
real_qa.r: California requires separate compensation for specific categories of time, and dividing the total paycheck by hours does not prove that each required component has been paid separately. For example, calculating $28.68 per hour average from mileage earnings may look fair, but if nonproductive time and rest periods require their own separate calculations and wage statement entries, those must be tracked and paid distinctly—averaging does not satisfy the legal requirement.
